0158               
0159               ; While we don't mean to USE the console ROM, for interrupts we
0160               ; are forced to interface with some of it. We need these addresses
0161               ; to minimize what it does so we can maximize our use of scratchpad.
0162               ; While I'd like to use the cassette hook - requires only 10 instructions
0163               ; and only uses 6 words of scratchpad, we can't here because it
0164               ; loses the return address, meaning you can only use it if you
0165               ; know where your LIMI 2 is and interrupts are otherwise disabled. So
0166               ; we have to use the longer but more standard interrupt hook, which also
0167               ; reads VDP status for us (no choice).
0168               
0169      8379     intcnt              equ >8379   ; interrupt counter byte, adds 1 (from GPLWS r14) every frame
0170      837B     vdp_status          equ >837B   ; VDP status byte mirror
0171      83C2     intwsr1             equ >83c2   ; INT WS R1  - interrupt control flags - must be >8000
0172      83C4     intwsr2             equ >83c4   ; INT WS R2  - address of user interrupt routine (point to int_handler)
0173      83D6     intwsr11            equ >83d6   ; screen timeout counter - must be odd (init to 1, is inct every frame)
0174      83DA     intwsr13            equ >83da   ; INT WS R13 - used for interrupt call (word)
0175      83DC     intwsr14            equ >83dc   ; INT WS R14 - used for interrupt call (word)
0176      83DE     intwsr15            equ >83de   ; INT WS R15 - used for interrupt call (word)
0177      83F6     gplwsr11            equ >83f6   ; GPL WS R11 - return address to interrupt ROM (not used, but overwritten each int)
0178      83F8     gplwsr12            equ >83f8   ; GPL WS R12 - used for cassette test and interrupt hook test (zeroed each int)
0179      83FA     gplwsr13            equ >83fa   ; GPL WS R13 - used in my interrupt handler
0180      83FC     gplwsr14            equ >83fc   ; GPL WS R14 - flags used to detect cassette - must be >0108 (or at least >0020 clear)
0181      83FE     gplwsr15            equ >83fe   ; GPL WS R15 - base address of VDP for status read - must be >8C02

0470               ; Load sprite definitions: Sprite number in R4, CPU data in R0, count of sprites in R5 (MSB)
0471               ; Original: pointer = sprite number, temp = CPU address, a = number sprites
0472               ; Note: sprites are all expected to be double-size 16x16, 32 bytes each, so sprite char 1 is character 4
0473               ; Sprite pattern table at >3800
0474               define_sprite
0475 A1DA C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0476 A1DC C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; Source data.
0477 A1DE C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; VRAM target.
0478 A1E0 0A50  26     sla r0,5            ; sprite number times 32 for bytes
0479 A1E2 0220  22     ai r0,>3800         ; add VDP base
     A1E4 3800     
0480 A1E6 C0C5  18     mov r5,r3		; Length.
0481 A1E8 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make int
0482 A1EA 0A53  26     sla r3,5            ; count times 32
0483 A1EC 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A1EE 0000     
0484 A1F0 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM          ; do the copy
     A1F2 A076     
0485 A1F4 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A1F6 0002     
0486 A1F8 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0487               
0488               ; Load character definitions: Char number in R1, CPU data in R2, count in R3 (MSB)
0489               ; Original: pointer = char number, temp = CPU address, a = number chars
0490               ; Note this loads the pattern three times if in bitmap mode (MODE&0x04)
0491               ; Pattern table at >0000
0492               define_char
0493 A1FA C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0494 A1FC C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; source data
0495 A1FE C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; move input to scratch
0496 A200 0A30  22     sla r0,3            ; char number times 8 (VDP base is 0, so already there)
0497 A202 C0C5  18     mov r5,r3
0498 A204 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make word
0499 A206 0A33  22     sla r3,3            ; count times 8
0500 A208 D160  30     movb @mode,r5       ; get mode flags
     A20A 834E     
0501 A20C 0245  22     andi r5,>0800
     A20E 0800     
0502 A210 1607  14     jne !1              ; not in bitmap mode, do a single copy
0503               
0504 A212 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A214 0000     
0505 A216 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM3         ; do the triple copy
     A218 A090     
0506 A21A 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A21C 0002     
0507 A21E 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0508               
0509               !1
0510 A220 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A222 0000     
0511 A224 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM          ; do the single copy
     A226 A076     
0512 A228 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A22A 0002     
0513 A22C 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0514               
0515               ; Load bitmap color definitions: Char number in R1, CPU data in R2, count in R3 (MSB)
0516               ; Original: pointer = char number, temp = CPU address, a = number chars
0517               ; Note: always does the triple copy. Color table at >2000
0518               define_color
0519 A22E C20B  18     mov r11,r8          ; save return
0520 A230 C080  18     mov r0,r2           ; source data
0521 A232 C004  18     mov r4,r0           ; move input to scratch
0522 A234 0A30  22     sla r0,3            ; char number times 8
0523 A236 0220  22     ai r0,>2000         ; add base address
     A238 2000     
0524 A23A C0C5  18     mov r5,r3
0525 A23C 0983  32     srl r3,8            ; make word
0526 A23E 0A33  22     sla r3,3            ; count times 8
0527 A240 0300  22     limi 0              ; ints off
     A242 0000     
0528 A244 06A0  32     bl @LDIRVM3         ; do the triple copy
     A246 A090     
0529 A248 0300  22     limi 2              ; ints on
     A24A 0002     
0530 A24C 0458  20     b *r8               ; back to caller
0531               
0532               ; Update sprite entry - copy data (4 bytes) to sprite table mirror at sprites
0533               ; R4 = sprite number, R5 = byte 1, r6 = byte 2, r7 = byte 3, r0 = byte 4 (all MSB)
0534               ; Original: A = sprite number, source data at sprite_data
0535               update_sprite
0536 A24E 0984  32     srl r4,8            ; make word
0537 A250 0A24  20     sla r4,2            ; x4 for address
0538 A252 0224  22     ai r4,sprites       ; sprite mirror address
     A254 2000     
0539 A256 DD05  32     movb r5,*r4+        ; move bytes
0540 A258 DD06  32     movb r6,*r4+        ; move bytes
0541 A25A DD07  32     movb r7,*r4+        ; move bytes
0542 A25C DD00  32     movb r0,*r4+        ; move bytes
0543 A25E 045B  20     b *r11
0544               
0545               ; SGN R0 - return 1, -1 or 0 as 16 bit
0546               _sgn16
0547 A260 C000  18     mov r0,r0       ; check for zero
0548 A262 1306  14     jeq !1          ; if yes, we're done
0549 A264 0240  22     andi r0,>8000   ; check for negative
     A266 8000     
0550 A268 1302  14     jeq !2          ; was not
0551 A26A 0700  14     seto r0         ; was negative, make it -1
0552 A26C 045B  20     b *r11          ; back to caller
0553               !2
0554 A26E 0580  14     inc r0          ; we know it was zero, and we want 1
0555               !1
0556 A270 045B  20     b *r11          ; back to caller
0557               
0558               ; 16-bit signed modulo. R1 % R2 = R0 - 9900 doesn't do signed divide
0559               ; original was stack%stack=YYAA
0560               ; Remainder is negative if the dividend was negative
0561               _mod16s
0562 A272 04C0  14     clr r0          ; make dividend 32-bit
0563 A274 C082  18     mov r2,r2       ; check divisor for zero
0564 A276 130A  14     jeq !1
0565 A278 0742  18     abs r2          ; make sure divisor is positive
0566 A27A C041  18     mov r1,r1       ; check sign of dividend
0567 A27C 1505  14     jgt !2          ; go do the faster positive version
0568               
0569 A27E 0741  18     abs r1          ; was negative, make it positive
0570 A280 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the division => r2=quotient, r3=remainder
0571 A282 0501  14     neg r1          ; make remainder negative
0572 A284 C001  18     mov r1,r0       ; into r0
0573 A286 045B  20     b *r11
0574               
0575               !2
0576 A288 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the division => r2=quotient, r3=remainder
0577 A28A C001  18     mov r1,r0       ; into r0
0578               !1
0579 A28C 045B  20     b *r11
0580               
0581               ; 16-bit signed divide. R1 / R2 = R0 - 9900 doesn't do signed divide
0582               ; original was stack/stack=YYAA
0583               ; Remainder is negative if the signs differ
0584               _div16s
0585 A28E 04C0  14     clr r0          ; make dividend 32-bit
0586 A290 C0C2  18     mov r2,r3       ; check divisor for zero
0587 A292 1308  14     jeq !1          ;
0588 A294 28C1  18     xor r1,r3
0589 A296 0742  18     abs r2
0590 A298 0741  18     abs r1          ; might as well make them positive now that we have copies
0591 A29A 3C02 128     div r2,r0       ; do the divide => r0=quotient, r1=remainder
0592 A29C 0243  22     andi r3,>8000   ; mask out sign bit
     A29E 8000     
0593 A2A0 1301  14     jeq !1          ; skip ahead to positive version
0594               
0595 A2A2 0500  14     neg r0          ; negate the result
0596               !1
0597 A2A4 045B  20     b *r11
0598               
0599               ; Random number generator - return in R0, (complex one uses R3,R4, simpler one only R0)
0600               ; Original output into YYAA
0601               random
0628               ; simpler one from dreamcast days...

     A2A8 834C

0631 A2AC 1702  14     jnc .rand1          ; jump if no 1

     A2B0 A2B8     
0633               .rand1
0634 A2B2 C800  30     mov r0,@lfsr        ; save the output
     A2B4 834C     
0635 A2B6 045B  20     b *r11
0636               rmask
0637 A2B8 B400         data >b400          ; mask for 16 bit
0639               
0640               ; Set SN Frequency: R0=frequency code, R2=channel command (MSB)
0641               ; Original: A=least significant byte  X=channel command  Y=most significant byte
0642               sn76489_freq
0643 A2BA C0C0  18     mov r0,r3

     A2BE 000F

     A2C6 8400

0649 A2CA 0240  22     andi r0,>003f
     A2CC 003F

0651 A2D0 D800  30     movb r0,@SOUND  ; most significant byte
     A2D2 8400     
0652 A2D4 045B  20     b *r11
0653               
0654               ; Set SN volume: R0=volume (MSB, inverse of attenuation), R2=channel command (MSB)

0656               sn76489_vol

     A2E0 8400

0832               
0833               ; this is where interrupts happen every frame
0834               ; Unlike a normal TI application, this one runs with interrupts ON,
0835               ; so all operations need to be sure to protect VDP address with LIMI 0,
0836               ; as well as any operations that might need to manipulate data managed
0837               ; by this interrupt. We enter via the normal user hook, so WP is on
0838               ; GPLWS, interrupts are off, and the VDP is already reset and status
0839               ; stashed on vdp_status (>837b). Our return address to the ROM is in
0840               ; r11, but we are NOT going to use it so that we don't need to reserve
0841               ; r8 for whatever nonsense it does. That means we need to load intws
0842               ; and RTWP ourselves at the end. We are on our own workspace so we
0843               ; don't have to worry about the main app's workspace.
0844               int_handler
0845               ; first copy the sprite table
0846 A48E 02E0  18     lwpi myintwp        ; separate safe workspace
     A490 8320     
0847               
0849 A492 C820  46     mov @>7ffe,@saved_bank  ; save bank switch page
     A494 7FFE     
     A496 8352     
0851               
0852 A498 020B  20     li r11,>005b        ; >1b00 with the write bit added, and byte flipped
     A49A 005B     
0853 A49C D80B  30     movb r11,@VDPWADR   ; SAL address
     A49E 8C02     
0854 A4A0 06CB  14     swpb r11
0855 A4A2 D80B  30     movb r11,@VDPWADR   ; going to copy the sprite table to VDP
     A4A4 8C02     
0856               
0857 A4A6 D2E0  30     movb @mode,r11
     A4A8 834E     
0858 A4AA 024B  22     andi r11,>0400      ; if bit >04 (inhibit flicker) is cleared, jump ahead to rotate
     A4AC 0400     
0859 A4AE 130A  14     jeq !4
0860               
0861 A4B0 04CB  14     clr r11             ; else we're going to just write it straight across
0862 A4B2 020C  20     li r12,128
     A4B4 0080     
0863 A4B6 020D  20     li r13,sprites
     A4B8 2000     
0864               !7
0865 A4BA D83D  40     movb *r13+,@VDPWDATA
     A4BC 8C00     
0866 A4BE 060C  14     dec r12
0867 A4C0 16FC  14     jne -!7
0868 A4C2 101B  14     jmp !5
0869               
0870               !4
0871 A4C4 D2E0  30     movb @flicker,r11   ; here we write it rotated every frame
     A4C6 834F     
0872 A4C8 022B  22     ai r11,>0400
     A4CA 0400     
0873 A4CC 024B  22     andi r11,>7f00
     A4CE 7F00     
0874 A4D0 D80B  30     movb r11,@flicker
     A4D2 834F     
0875 A4D4 06CB  14     swpb r11            ; make count
0876 A4D6 020C  20     li r12,32           ; count
     A4D8 0020     
0877               
0878               !6
0879 A4DA 022B  22     ai r11,sprites        ; this is still faster than separate incs
     A4DC 2000

0890               ; next read the joysticks - output needs to be 21xxLDRU - 1 and 2 are button and button2 respectively
0891               ; We don't have a button 2. We also need to read the keyboard and fill in key1_data. key2_data we
0892               ; will leave unused. Note key1_data expects Coleco-style 0-9,10-*,11-#,15=not pressed, but we can throw
0893               ; everything else as ASCII. We could do a split keyboard for 2 players, but I guess we'll leave it for now.

     A522 0006

1018               ; given a joystick read in r13, return bits in r12

1929               ; The stack is simulated using R10. It's not used in
1930               ; these functions but the compiled code will need it.
1931               ; To push: dect r10, mov r0,*r10
1932               ; To pop:  mov *r10+,r0
1933               ; However, for JSR a function is helpful - call this like:
1934               ; bl @jsr
1935               ; data <function_address>
1936               jsr
1937 A980 C3BB  30     mov *r11+,r14       ; get the jump address
1938 A982 064A  14     dect r10            ; make room on stack
1939 A984 C68B  30     mov r11,*r10        ; save return address
1940 A986 069E  24     bl *r14             ; new subroutine call, we can come back here
1941 A988 C2FA  30     mov *r10+,r11       ; get real return off stack - warning, all basic functions do this inline rather than return
1942 A98A 045B  20     b *r11              ; back to caller
1943

     A99A 8802

1984               ;;; CVBasic code starts here
1985               	; 	' ==========================================================================
1986               	; 	' KEYSTONE KAPERS -- CVBasic, dual target TI-99/4A + ColecoVision.
1987               	; 	'
1988               	; 	' Garry Kitchen's 1983 Activision game. See DESIGN.md; 0 records the
1989               	; 	' research and the four places the sources disagree.
1990               	; 	'
1991               	; 	' Fifty seconds to run Harry Hooligan down inside a department store eight
1992               	; 	' screens wide and four levels tall, before he reaches the roof.
1993               	; 	'
1994               	; 	' THE THREE DECISIONS THIS FILE IS BUILT ON, all from DESIGN.md:
1995               	; 	'
1996               	; 	'   * THE VIEW FLIPS, IT DOES NOT SCROLL. Eight discrete screens; crossing
1997               	; 	'     an edge blits the next one. The per-frame budget never pays for the
1998               	; 	'     store at all -- RallyX repaints 576 chars every camera cell and had
1999               	; 	'     to have all its movement rewritten to survive that.
2000               	; 	'   * A SCREEN IS EXACTLY 256 PX, so an actor's x within its screen is one
2001               	; 	'     unsigned byte. No 16-bit world coordinate exists in this program.
2002               	; 	'   * ZERO PER-FRAME VDP READS. An actor's floor is an index into flry(),
2003               	; 	'     never a question asked of the screen, so the Ms. Pac-Man trap
2004               	; 	'     (actors x per-actor search) is absent by construction.
2005               	; 	'
2006               	; 	' The rules that shaped the code, all from CLAUDE.md 3A, because every one
2007               	; 	' of them fails SILENTLY:
2008               	; 	'
2009               	; 	'   * A plain variable is 8-BIT and a CONST over 255 TRUNCATES. Every
2010               	; 	'     name-table offset past row 7 is a #var or a bare literal.
2011               	; 	'   * Every #var comparison is UNSIGNED.
2012               	; 	'   * `<cmp> AND <cmp>` is miscompiled by the 9900 backend. Nested IFs.
2013               	; 	'   * A sprite at y=208 TERMINATES the sprite list. Hidden sprites go 209.
2014               	; 	'   * A GOSUB left by GOTO never pops. Death, catch and escape are STATES
2015               	; 	'     set in a routine and acted on at the top of the main loop.
2016               	; 	'   * MPY clobbers r0. Nothing here multiplies into an index -- the tables
2017               	; 	'     tsrc()/bdst()/lv8() exist precisely so that no multiply is needed on
2018               	; 	'     a path that reads the result back.
2019               	; 	' ==========================================================================
2020               	;
2021               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- BANKING
2022               	; 	' THE ART AND THE STORE MAP LIVE IN ROM BANK 1 ON THE TI. The fixed area
2023               	; 	' is 24,336 bytes -- three 8,112-byte loader pages -- and unbanked this
2024               	; 	' program filled 24,304 of them, so there was no room left for anything at
2025               	; 	' all. `linkticart` does not warn when you exceed it; it silently discards
2026               	; 	' the top of the image, and what goes missing is whatever sits nearest the
2027               	; 	' end, usually a DATA block rather than code. Nothing errors.
2028               	; 	'
2029               	; 	' WHAT IS SAFE TO BANK. Everything moved here is read at SETUP (the
2030               	; 	' DEFINE CHAR / DEFINE SPRITE calls) or on a screen crossing (the template
2031               	; 	' blit and the escalator's phase tables) -- and, because there is exactly
2032               	; 	' ONE data bank and it is selected ONCE at startup and never switched, it
2033               	; 	' stays mapped for the life of the program. The rule in CLAUDE.md 3A is
2034               	; 	' about SWITCHING inside a frame or under the vblank ISR; with a single
2035               	; 	' permanently-selected bank there is no switch to miss. A missed
2036               	; 	' BANK SELECT would return bytes from the wrong page with no error at
2037               	; 	' build or run time, which is why there is only one and it is set before
2038               	; 	' anything reads from it.
2039               	; 	'
2040               	; 	' BANK ROM 128 sizes ColecoVision's Megacart mapper, NOT the TI cart --
2041               	; 	' that comes from how many bank files the assembler emits -- and it is
2042               	; 	' one of only four values the compiler accepts (128/256/512/1024).
2043               	; 	' The whole thing is gated on TI994A: the Coleco build is Z80 and roughly
2044               	; 	' half the size, so it neither needs banking nor wants to become a
2045               	; 	' Megacart image.
2046               	; 	#if TI994A
2047               	; 	BANK ROM 128
2048               	; 	#endif
2049               	; 	CONST SPRHID = 209		' NOT 208 -- 208 terminates the sprite list
2050      00D1     const_SPRHID	equ >00d1
2051               	;
2052               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------------- geometry
2053               	; 	' A band is 5 rows: 4 rows of air (32 px) over one floor slab. Standing
2054               	; 	' Kelly is 16 px, so headroom is 16 px and the jump apex is 14 -- two
2055               	; 	' short of the ceiling, because an arc that bonks is silently truncated.
2056               	; 	' 4 px/frame = 240 px/s. At 2 it was not merely sluggish, it was
2057               	; 	' ARITHMETICALLY TOO SLOW: the climb is three traverses = 6,144 px, which
2058               	; 	' at 2 px/frame is 51 seconds of pure running against a 50-second clock,
2059               	; 	' before a single obstacle, escalator ride or catch. At 3 it is 34 s --
2060               	; 	' and 34 s was still wrong, for a reason a per-actor speed check cannot
2061               	; 	' see: HARRY'S CLIMB IS ALSO 34 s (DESIGN.md 4a). Kelly being 1.5x faster
2062               	; 	' bought nothing, because Harry's route is two thirds the length of
2063               	; 	' Kelly's -- he spawns beside floor 2's escalator and effectively skips a
2064               	; 	' traverse. A chase resolves on PATH / SPEED, not on speed, and the two
2065               	; 	' quotients were equal, so pursuit on foot could never close. At 4 the
2066               	; 	' climb is 25 s against Harry's 45, and the elevator buys back more.
2067               	; 	CONST WALKSP = 4		' px per PASS -- the old unit, kept only for
2068      0004     const_WALKSP	equ >0004
2069               	; 					' the checkers' arithmetic and the comments
2070               	; 					' that quote it. Nothing moves by it now.
2071               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS OF A PIXEL PER FRAME, which is what he actually walks by.
2072               	; 	'
2073               	; 	' HIS OLD BEST-CASE SPEED, MADE CONSTANT -- not his old average. WALKSP was
2074               	; 	' 4 px per loop PASS, so what he actually did depended on the screen: 104 px/s
2075               	; 	' on a light one at 26 passes/s, 80 px/s on the lift and escalator screens at
2076               	; 	' 20. Matching the MEASURED AVERAGE of 23.8 passes/s gave 95.6 px/s (102/64),
2077               	; 	' which is the same average and an 8% loss on exactly the screens a chase
2078               	; 	' spends most of its time crossing -- the crook was already per-frame and did
2079               	; 	' not change, so the ratio that decides the chase quietly dropped. Played, it
2080               	; 	' read as only just catching him on the last screen.
2081               	; 	'
2082               	; 	' 111/64 is 104.1 px/s: his best case, everywhere. He is now at least as fast
2083               	; 	' as he ever was on any screen rather than faster on some and slower on
2084               	; 	' others, and the chase margin goes from 10.6 s to 17.3 s.
2085               	; 	CONST KWALK64 = 111
2086      006F     const_KWALK64	equ >006f
2087               	; 	' The bounce phase, in sixty-fourths of a phase per frame. 32 phases at
2088               	; 	' 25/64 per frame is 1.37 s an arc, against the 1.35 s one phase per pass
2089               	; 	' gives at 23.8 passes a second.
2090               	; 	CONST BOUNCE64 = 25
2091      0019     const_BOUNCE64	equ >0019
2092               	; 	CONST XWALL = 232		' furthest left edge at the store's east wall
2093      00E8     const_XWALL	equ >00e8
2094               	; 	' AND THE ROOF HAS NO EAST WALL, so the crook runs two characters further.
2095               	; 	' Floors 1-3 end in an ENDWALL character at column 31 and XWALL stops an
2096               	; 	' actor just short of it. The roof does not have one -- its east end is the
2097               	; 	' edge of the BUILDING, the skyline carries on to the screen edge, and the
2098               	; 	' round ends with him going over it.
2099               	; 	'
2100               	; 	' 252 IS FOUR PIXELS SHORT OF THE LAST COLUMN, and that is the point: his
2101               	; 	' sprite is 16 px wide, so at 240 he stands flush against the edge FULLY
2102               	; 	' VISIBLE and then simply stops existing -- `do_escape` runs `hide_all` on
2103               	; 	' the same pass. At 252 twelve of those sixteen pixels are already clipped
2104               	; 	' off the screen when he goes, so he reads as having walked off the roof
2105               	; 	' rather than having been deleted from it. The arrival test allows 6 px of
2106               	; 	' slack, so the last frame he is drawn on shows between one and four
2107               	; 	' columns of him.
2108               	; 	'
2109               	; 	' 255 is the true ceiling and buys three more pixels; 252 keeps a little
2110               	; 	' headroom for an off-by-one in whatever edits this next.
2111               	; 	'
2112               	; 	' This is only reachable because the EXIT DOOR that stood at columns 28-30
2113               	; 	' was removed (genstore.py, the roof's east template). Six cells of white
2114               	; 	' box on dark blue, reading on screen as purple dots -- it was asked about
2115               	; 	' as a graphical fault, it says he leaves through a doorway rather than off
2116               	; 	' a roof, and it was exactly where he used to stop.
2117               	; 	CONST XROOF = 252
2118      00FC     const_XROOF	equ >00fc
2119               	; 	CONST XWALW = 8			' nearest left edge at the west wall
2120      0008     const_XWALW	equ >0008
2121               	; 	CONST STANDH = 24		' Kelly standing -- TWO SPRITES tall
2122      0018     const_STANDH	equ >0018
2123               	; 	' KELLY DUCKED. It was 8 px, which is not a crouch -- it is a squash, with
2124               	; 	' no room to draw a figure bending in a DIRECTION. 11 px is, and the
2125               	; 	' biplane is raised to match (obh below, and the hitbox in coll_obst):
2126               	; 	' with the plane at 16..22 an 11 px crouch passes five pixels under it and
2127               	; 	' a 24 px standing Kop does not. The apex is 14, so a jump still cannot
2128               	; 	' clear it either -- the plane stays the one obstacle that must be ducked.
2129               	; 	'
2130               	; 	' AND 11 IS THE CEILING, not a preference. Duckable means the obstacle
2131               	; 	' clears the crouch, jumpable means it clears under the apex; raising the
2132               	; 	' crouch raises the duckable floor, so past 11 a band of beach-ball
2133               	; 	' heights is neither. A sweep of every crouch height against every ball
2134               	; 	' hitbox puts the limit at 11, and shrinking the ball does not move it --
2135               	; 	' the apex is what binds. assets/checkball.py fails the build on it.
2136               	; 	CONST DUCKH = 11		' Kelly ducked -- bent over, not squashed
2137      000B     const_DUCKH	equ >000b
2138               	; 	CONST CATCHR = 12
2139      000C     const_CATCHR	equ >000c
2140               	; 	' HOW CLOSE VERTICALLY A CATCH NEEDS. A floor is a whole storey apart, so
2141               	; 	' anything under a character row means they are genuinely level; a rider
2142               	; 	' eight pixels up a flight is already clear of a Kop standing beside it.
2143               	; 	CONST CATCHV = 8		' catch / hit radius, centre to centre
2144      0008     const_CATCHV	equ >0008
2145               	;
2146               	; 	' Kelly states
2147               	; 	CONST ST_RUN = 0
2148      0000     const_ST_RUN	equ >0000
2149               	; 	CONST ST_JUMP = 1
2150      0001     const_ST_JUMP	equ >0001
2151               	; 	CONST ST_DUCK = 2
2152      0002     const_ST_DUCK	equ >0002
2153               	; 	CONST ST_ESC = 3		' riding an escalator -- no input, invincible
2154      0003     const_ST_ESC	equ >0003
2155               	; 	CONST ST_ELEV = 4		' inside the car     -- no input, invincible
2156      0004     const_ST_ELEV	equ >0004

2159               	; 	CONST OB_CART = 1
2160      0001     const_OB_CART	equ >0001
2161               	; 	CONST OB_BALL = 2
2162      0002     const_OB_BALL	equ >0002

2497               	; 	' HOW FAR THE SECOND HAZARD ON A FLOOR TRAILS THE FIRST, in pixels.
2498               	; 	'
2499               	; 	' THERE ARE ONLY TWO SAFE ANSWERS. Kelly closes on an oncoming hazard at
2500               	; 	' (KWALK64 + its speed)/64 px a FRAME -- 2.53 at the slow speed, 2.92 at
2501               	; 	' the fast one -- and the jump arc holds its apex for 9 frames and is
2502               	; 	' airborne for 28. So:
2503               	; 	'
2504               	; 	'   <= 22 px   ONE JUMP CLEARS BOTH -- the pair drifts under the apex
2505               	; 	'   >= 82 px   he can LAND BETWEEN them -- a whole jump fits in the gap
2506               	; 	'
2507               	; 	' Anything in between is the dangerous middle: too far to clear together,
2508               	; 	' too close to land between. The gap shipped at 46 px west of the lift and
2509               	; 	' 70 px east of it -- 46 is inside the first window and 70 is squarely in
2510               	; 	' that middle, which is the asymmetry that got reported. It then shipped at
2511               	; 	' 20, in the first window, which is a pair taken as ONE obstacle.
2512               	; 	'
2513               	; 	' 104 IS MEASURED FROM THE ORIGINAL, not chosen. A frame-by-frame census of
2514               	; 	' a full 2600 playthrough (assets/ref2600/hazards.md) finds that two moving
2515               	; 	' hazards on one floor are NEVER closer than 108 px in our scale -- not once
2516               	; 	' in 21 levels -- and that its static radios come as close as 54. Our own
2517               	; 	' arc independently puts the land-between threshold at 82 px for a mover and
2518               	; 	' 49 for a static one, so the original sits just above both, from evidence
2519               	; 	' that knows nothing about this jump. That is the run / jump / run / jump
2520               	; 	' the reviewer described, and it is what the 20 px pair was not.
2521               	; 	'
2522               	; 	' THE PRICE IS SLOT 0's JITTER, and it is arithmetic, not a choice. `stag`
2523               	; 	' is distance from the FAR edge, so the second hazard sits GAP px nearer the
2524               	; 	' wall the player walks in through. He needs a reaction budget there
2525               	; 	' (checkspace.py's WARNPX, 120 px), and 120 + 104 = 224 of the 240 px of
2526               	; 	' placeable floor -- so the pair can only slide 16 px. Hence HAZMASK below.
2527               	; 	' That is not less faithful than what it replaces: the original places its
2528               	; 	' radios on exactly THREE fixed positions per floor, so it has no jitter at
2529               	; 	' all. assets/checkspace.py checks the gap, the entry distance and the
2530               	; 	' offset rule together, and checkspace_test.py proves it still rejects 70
2531               	; 	' and 176 -- and now 71, which only the FASTEST hazard can see.
2532               	; 	CONST HAZGAP = 104
2533      0068     const_HAZGAP	equ >0068
2534               	; 	' Slot 0's stagger mask ONCE A FLOOR CAN CARRY TWO. Before that a floor has
2535               	; 	' one hazard, the pair arithmetic above does not apply, and slot 0 keeps its
2536               	; 	' full 64 px of jitter -- which is most of the early game, where the player
2537               	; 	' meets the fewest hazards and variety is worth the most.
2538               	; 	CONST HAZMASK = 15
2539      000F     const_HAZMASK	equ >000f
2540               	; 	CONST ELDOOR = 15		' frames the doors spend part-open
2541      000F     const_ELDOOR	equ >000f
2542               	; 	CONST ELOPEN = 85		' = ELWAIT - ELDOOR, as a literal: a CONST
2543      0055     const_ELOPEN	equ >0055
2544               	; 					' built from other CONSTs is exactly the
2545               	; 					' folded-constant trap in CLAUDE.md 3A
2546               	;
2547               	; 	' escalator boarding zones, in CENTRE-x pixels
2548               	; 	' ESCALATOR BOARDING ZONES, IN PIXELS, AND THEY TRACK THE ART.
2549               	; 	' The flight is drawn as four rows of two characters stepping two columns
2550               	; 	' per row: west runs cols 1-2 (top) down to 7-8 (foot), east runs 29-30
2551               	; 	' (top) down to 23-24 (foot). These zones ARE those columns x8. When the
2552               	; 	' escalator art changed from a filled triangle to a stepped flight the
2553               	; 	' foot moved, and a boarding zone left where it was would put the player
2554               	; 	' on a staircase that is not under them -- no error, just a floor that
2555               	; 	' teleports you when you walk over an empty patch of it.
2556               	; 	' THESE ARE THE DRAWN STEPS, in screen pixels. The flight is fifteen
2557               	; 	' characters wide: its foot tread sits at x 95-103 (west) and 152-160
2558               	; 	' (east), its head tread at 23-31 and 224-232. An actor rides between
2559               	; 	' those, so the numbers here are the ART's, and moving the art without
2560               	; 	' moving them puts the rider beside the escalator rather than on it.
2561               	; 	' THE RIDER STANDS ON A STEP, and everything about the ride follows from
2562               	; 	' WHICH ONE. The staircase is a straight line -- a step 4 px higher is 8
2563               	; 	' px further along it -- so one number, the step's height above the floor
2564               	; 	' being left, fixes both the rider's x and the rest of the ride:
2565               	; 	'
2566               	; 	'     west  klx = 99 - 2*height        east  klx = 140 + 2*height
2567               	; 	'
2568               	; 	' The bottom step is 4 px up, so a rider walking on boards at klx = 91
2569               	; 	' (west) or 148 (east); the head step is 40 up, so the ride ends at 19 or
2570               	; 	' 220. Those are the ART's numbers -- the foot tread is drawn at x 95-103
2571               	; 	' west and 152-160 east, the head tread at 23-31 and 224-232 -- so moving
2572               	; 	' the art without moving these puts the rider beside the staircase.
2573               	; 	'
2574               	; 	' THE PHASE MATTERS. The steps climb 1 px a frame and the animation runs
2575               	; 	' four 1 px phases, so the bottom step is 4 + escp px up, not 4. Boarding
2576               	; 	' without that term leaves the feet up to 3 px out of register with the
2577               	; 	' tread and the whole ride drifts, which is exactly what "he floats
2578               	; 	' beside the steps" looked like.
2579               	; 	CONST ESCFX = 91		' west foot: rider's x when boarding
2580      005B     const_ESCFX	equ >005b
2581               	; 	CONST ESCFXE = 148		' east foot
2582      0094     const_ESCFXE	equ >0094
2583               	; 	CONST ESCHX = 19		' west head: rider's x on arrival
2584      0013     const_ESCHX	equ >0013
2585               	; 	CONST ESCHXE = 220		' east head
2586      00DC     const_ESCHXE	equ >00dc
2587               	; 	CONST ESCRISE = 40		' floor to floor, and the ride's length
2588      0028     const_ESCRISE	equ >0028
2589               	;
2590               	; 	' TIMER UNITS PER KROOK, AND A UNIT IS NOT A SECOND. Measured off the
2591               	; 	' reference video (DESIGN.md 0m): the original counts 50 down to 0 and a
2592               	; 	' unit lasts 1.99 s, so a round is about 100 seconds. TICKFR below is
2593               	; 	' what makes it so here.
2594               	; 	CONST TIMEL = 50		' timer units per Krook
2595      0032     const_TIMEL	equ >0032
2596               	; 	' FRAMES PER TIMER UNIT. 120, not 60, and this is not cosmetic -- it is
2597               	; 	' what makes a round finishable. Everything that MOVES in this game is
2598               	; 	' paced per loop PASS, and the loop runs about 25 passes a second, so
2599               	; 	' Kelly's 4 px a pass is ~100 px/s (the reference's Kelly is 102, so the
2600               	; 	' speeds match). The timer, though, is paced by the frame DELTA -- real
2601               	; 	' wall-clock time. At 60 frames a unit the round was 50 real seconds
2602               	; 	' while Kelly's route to the roof takes about 72, so the clock ran out
2603               	; 	' before either of them could get there and every round ended on a
2604               	; 	' timeout. checkchase.py hid it by assuming 60 passes a second; it now
2605               	; 	' models the real rate.
2606               	; 	CONST TICKFR = 120
2607      0078     const_TICKFR	equ >0078
2608               	; 	' NINE TIMER UNITS -- not ten, and not nine seconds. Every source says a
2609               	; 	' cart, ball or radio costs "9 seconds", and what they mean is the number
2610               	; 	' on the HUD, because that is what the manual calls seconds. So the
2611               	; 	' DISPLAYED count drops by 9. A unit is about two real seconds
2612               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 0m), which makes one careless cart cost roughly eighteen --
2613               	; 	' close to a fifth of the round, and the reason the refractory latch
2614               	; 	' below matters so much.
2615               	; 	CONST HITPEN = 9		' timer units a cart / ball / radio costs
2616      0009     const_HITPEN	equ >0009
2617               	; 	' HOW LONG A HIT SOUNDS, IN LOOP PASSES -- and therefore how long the
2618               	; 	' store stands still for one. The two are the same number on purpose:
2619               	; 	' the freeze is meant to last exactly as long as the noise, so a change
2620               	; 	' to one that did not move the other would leave either a silent pause
2621               	; 	' or a sound playing over a resumed game. Passes, not frames, because
2622               	; 	' both counters are spent once per pass in sfx_tick and the main loop.
2623               	; 	CONST HITSND = 20
2624      0014     const_HITSND	equ >0014
2625               	; 	CONST HITREF = 45		' frames before the SAME obstacle can charge
2626      002D     const_HITREF	equ >002d
2627               	; 					' again. See coll_obst -- clearing the latch
2628               	; 					' on the first non-overlapping frame is not
2629               	; 					' enough, because a bouncing ball leaves
2630               	; 					' contact between bounces.
2631               	;
2632               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- tables
2633               	; 	DIM flry(4)			' floor surface y, by level
2634               	; 	DIM #bdst(4)			' band name-table offset, by level
2635               	; 	DIM #tsrc(15)			' template source offset, by template id
2636               	; 	' THE NES CANNOT READ ITS OWN VIDEO MEMORY BACK, so anything this
2637               	; 	' program does as read-modify-write needs the "read" to come from RAM
2638               	; 	' instead. WRTVRM on that target does not touch the PPU at all -- it
2639               	; 	' queues into PPUBUF for the NMI to flush -- so a read would be both
2640               	; 	' illegal during rendering and blind to everything still in the queue.
2641               	; 	'
2642               	; 	' The radar is the only read-modify-write on the PATTERN table: it ORs
2643               	; 	' pixel rows into its canvas characters, 208-255, eight bytes each.
2644               	; 	' 384 bytes of the NES's 1,227 free, and nothing on the other targets.
2645               	; 	#if NES
2646               	; 	DIM nsc(384)			' radar canvas pattern shadow
2647               	; 	#endif
2648               	; 	DIM lv8(4)			' lv*8, so no multiply lands on an index
2649               	; 	DIM jarc(32)			' the jump arc: 30 frames, apex 14
2650               	; 	DIM msk(8)
2651               	;
2652               	; 	' EIGHT obstacle slots -- TWO per band, and that number is forced.
2653               	; 	'
2654               	; 	' The VDP shows four sprites per scanline and DROPS the rest by slot
2655               	; 	' order; it does not flicker them, they simply are not there. Three per
2656               	; 	' band was sized against Kelly alone (1 + 3 = 4) and forgot that HARRY
2657               	; 	' can be on that band too -- and when he is, the fifth sprite on his
2658               	; 	' scanline is the highest-numbered obstacle, which vanishes while still
2659               	; 	' being solid. An invisible thing that costs nine seconds is the worst
2660               	; 	' failure in the game and it only happens when the crook is next to you,
2661               	; 	' which is exactly when you are not looking at the floor.
2662               	; 	'
2663               	; 	' Kelly (slot 0) + Harry (slot 1) + two obstacles = four. Provably never
2664               	; 	' dropped, on any band, in any situation.
2665               	; 	'
2666               	; 	' ...AND THAT CAP IS ABOUT SPRITES, WHICH A RADIO IS NOT. The scanline
2667               	; 	' limit is the whole argument above, and it does not reach the radio: a
2668               	; 	' radio is four CHARACTERS stamped into the name table by draw_radios, it
2669               	; 	' costs no sprite, and the VDP will happily draw a hundred of them on one
2670               	; 	' line. The original puts up to THREE on a floor (assets/ref2600/hazards.md
2671               	; 	' measures them at three fixed positions), and the reason we had two was
2672               	; 	' this comment being read as a limit on hazards when it is a limit on
2673               	; 	' sprites.
2674               	; 	'
2675               	; 	' So there are TWELVE slots in two groups, and the split is deliberate:
2676               	; 	'
2677               	; 	'   0-7    two per band, band*2 + slot -- ANY kind, and these are the ones
2678               	; 	'          that own sprites 8-15 (propellers 16-23). Untouched.
2679               	; 	'   8-11   ONE per band, 8 + band -- RADIO OR EMPTY, never a sprite.
2680               	; 	'
2681               	; 	' Keeping the new slots in their own block rather than making the stride
2682               	; 	' three is what leaves draw_obst's `FOR di = 0 TO 7` and its `ds = di + 8`
2683               	; 	' exactly as they were. A stride of three would have scattered the
2684               	; 	' sprite-bearing slots to 0,1,3,4,6,7,9,10 and every sprite number in the
2685               	; 	' game would have had to be recomputed -- to place a thing that does not
2686               	; 	' use one.
2687               	; 	DIM obk(12)			' kind, 0 = empty
2688               	; 	DIM obx(12)			' x within the screen
2689               	; 	DIM obd(12)			' 0 = moving left, 1 = right
2690               	; 	DIM obh(12)			' art-bottom height above the slab
2691               	; 	DIM obc(12)			' cell column, radios only -- they are chars
2692               	; 	DIM obp(12)			' bounce phase, balls only
2693               	; 	DIM obht(12)			' hit refractory, per obstacle -- see coll_obst
2694               	;
2695               	; 	DIM cok(4)			' this screen's collectible, per band
2696               	; 	DIM coc(4)			' its column
2697               	; 	DIM takn(4)			' 32 bits: which bands have been cleaned out
2698               	;
2699               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- state
2700               	; 	' Kelly
2701               	; 	' klv 0..3 (0 = floor 1, 3 = roof), klsc 0..7, klx 0..255
2702               	; 	' Harry the same. NOTHING in this program is a world coordinate.
2703               	;
2704               	; 	' EVERYTHING IS BUILT BEFORE THE TITLE IS DRAWN, NOT BEHIND IT.
2705               	; 	'
2706               	; 	' The opposite order was tried first, on the reasoning that only the font
2707               	; 	' is needed to put text on a screen: draw the title immediately, then
2708               	; 	' define the store characters, the store colours, the escalator deck, the
2709               	; 	' radar canvas and eight sprite sets while the player reads it. None of
2710               	; 	' that is touched until new_game, so nothing was out of order.
2711               	; 	'
2712               	; 	' IT MADE THE TITLE APPEAR SOONER AND ARRIVE DEAD. A third of a second of
2713               	; 	' a finished screen that was not yet reading the keyboard -- long enough to
2714               	; 	' swallow the first digit of 8-3-8, and reported as a start press that did
2715               	; 	' not take. A menu the player cannot act on is not up yet, whatever is
2716               	; 	' painted on it.
2717               	; 	'
2718               	; 	' So the work moved back in front. The screen appears later and is live on
2719               	; 	' the frame it appears, and the prompt printed on it is honest rather than
2720               	; 	' hopeful. The cost lands once, on a black screen at power-on, where there

2746               	; 	'

2748               	; 	' round starts and read_input sees it on the very first pass. jrel is
2749               	; 	' supposed to absorb that -- start_krook clears it, so the latch demands a
2750               	; 	' release before the first jump -- and in play it did not, reported twice.
2751               	; 	' Rather than keep reasoning about the order of two latches, this waits
2752               	; 	' for the thing itself: the key that said "start" is not in the buffer any

2754               	; 	'
2755               	; 	' CAPPED AT A SECOND, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE COUNTER. A stuck
2756               	; 	' or shorted fire line would otherwise hang the game on a black screen for
2757               	; 	' ever, which is exactly the mistake the ALPHA LOCK check made in its first
2758               	; 	' version -- refusing to start until a condition cleared that never would.

2843               	; 	' THE STORE STOPS FOR A HIT. THE CHASE DOES NOT.
2844               	; 	'
2845               	; 	' Nine seconds off the clock is the heaviest thing that happens in this
2846               	; 	' game and it used to happen in silence and in motion: the number
2847               	; 	' changed, a flash played, and the player kept running. Holding the
2848               	; 	' screen for exactly as long as the hit SOUNDS makes the penalty an event
2849               	; 	' rather than a bookkeeping entry -- the arcade's own idiom, and the
2850               	; 	' reason the 2600 original pauses here too.

2854               	; 	' those as well would turn the penalty into free time. It also keeps the
2855               	; 	' two things the player is racing on their own clocks, which is the whole
2856               	; 	' argument of section 0f-ter -- a pause that stopped the timer would make
2857               	; 	' the price of a hit depend on how long the pause happened to be.

2862               	; 	' under a moving Harry would slide him up a stationary staircase.

3007               	; setup_font:
3008               cvb_SETUP_FONT
3009               	; 	' Flicker stays OFF. CVBasic's is all-or-nothing -- it rotates all 32
3010               	; 	' slots, so Kelly would strobe too, and he is the one thing the player
3011               	; 	' must never lose. He is sprite 0 instead: the VDP drops the
3012               	; 	' HIGHEST-numbered sprites on an over-full scanline, so slot 0 is the
3013               	; 	' one slot that can never disappear.
3014               	; 	SPRITE FLICKER OFF
3015 ABA0 0200  20 	li r0,>0400
     ABA2 0400     
3016 ABA4 F800  30 	socb r0,@mode
     ABA6 834E     
3017               	;
3018               	; 	' THE ONE AND ONLY BANK SWITCH THE PROGRAM EVER MAKES, and it happens
3019               	; 	' here, before the first frame.
3020               	; 	'
3021               	; 	' There are two data banks now. Bank 1 holds everything read while the
3022               	; 	' game is running -- sprite and store art, the templates, the lookup
3023               	; 	' tables -- and it is selected at the end of this routine and never
3024               	; 	' changed again, so every VARPTR/PEEK read in the program is reading a
3025               	; 	' page that is permanently mapped. That is the property that makes
3026               	; 	' banking safe here: a missed BANK SELECT returns bytes from the wrong
3027               	; 	' page with no error at build or run time, so the safest number of
3028               	; 	' switches during play is none.
3029               	; 	'
3030               	; 	' Bank 2 exists to hold data that is read ONCE, at setup, and never
3031               	; 	' again. The font is exactly that: two DEFINEs copy it into VRAM and
3032               	; 	' nothing reads font_bits or font_col for the rest of the run. So it can
3033               	; 	' live on a page that is mapped for the length of those two statements.
3034               	; 	'
3035               	; 	' IF THIS EVER FAILS IT FAILS LOUDLY. Select the wrong bank here and the
3036               	; 	' font is garbage on the title screen, immediately and unmistakably --
3037               	; 	' which is the same diagnostic the font used to provide by staying out of
3038               	; 	' the banks altogether, recovered for free.
3039               	; 	#if TI994A
3040               	; 	BANK SELECT 2
3041 ABA8 04E0  34 	clr @>6008
     ABAA 6008     
3042               	; 	#endif
3043               	;
3044               	; 	DEFINE CHAR 32,59,font_bits
3045 ABAC 0204  20 	li r4,32
     ABAE 0020     
3046 ABB0 0205  20 	li r5,15104
     ABB2 3B00     
3047 ABB4 0200  20 	li r0,cvb_FONT_BITS
     ABB6 602A     
3048 ABB8 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     ABBA A980     
3049 ABBC A1FA     	data define_char
3050               	; 	' Without this the font keeps whatever CVBasic left in the colour table --
3051               	; 	' white on transparent -- which over a green store made the HUD unreadable.
3052               	; 	'
3053               	; 	' THIS WAS A VPOKE LOOP AND IT WAS THE SLOWEST THING IN THE BOOT: 1,416
3054               	; 	' writes of one constant, paced by 24 WAITs, which is what made the title
3055               	; 	' fill in visibly instead of appearing. DEFINE COLOR does the same job in a
3056               	; 	' single call with interrupts off, and it writes all three screen thirds
3057               	; 	' itself -- define_color always takes the LDIRVM3 triple-copy path, which is
3058               	; 	' also why esc_deck_col and floor0_colour below CANNOT use it: they patch
3059               	; 	' one third each.
3060               	; 	'
3061               	; 	' The table is 472 identical bytes (genfont.py emits it beside the glyphs).
3062               	; 	' It reads as waste and is not: it lives in the data bank, which had 860
3063               	; 	' bytes spare, while the loop it replaced cost time in the one place the
3064               	; 	' player is made to wait.
3065               	; 	DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col
3066 ABBE 0204  20 	li r4,32
     ABC0 0020     
3067 ABC2 0205  20 	li r5,15104
     ABC4 3B00     
3068 ABC6 0200  20 	li r0,cvb_FONT_COL
     ABC8 6202     
3069 ABCA 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     ABCC A980     
3070 ABCE A22E     	data define_color
3071               	;
3072               	; 	' AND THE TITLE'S DISPLAY FACE, WHICH IS HERE FOR THE SAME REASON THE
3073               	; 	' FONT IS. Forty characters -- ten letters, four cells each -- drawn at
3074               	; 	' 16x16 so the game's name reads as a name rather than as a line of body
3075               	; 	' text. It is 640 bytes of pattern and colour and bank 1 had 370 free, so
3076               	; 	' it could not go there; it did not need to, because it is read ONCE, by
3077               	; 	' these two statements, and never again.
3078               	; 	'
3079               	; 	' Loading it inside the bank-2 window the font already opens means the
3080               	; 	' program still makes exactly ONE bank switch in its life.
3081               	; 	' IN TWO PIECES, AND THE SPLIT IS NOT TIDINESS. The character table has
3082               	; 	' 0..31, 91..95 and 182..207 free -- sixty-three codes, but the longest
3083               	; 	' run is thirty-two and the face needs forty. Loading it as one block at
3084               	; 	' 182 ran it into the RADAR CANVAS at 208, and S and T came out as the
3085               	; 	' scanner's green diagonals on a screen with no radar on it.
3086               	; 	'
3087               	; 	' The arguments come from titleface.FREE_RUNS; gentitle.py prints them
3088               	; 	' into the top of titlefont.bas and checkchars.py verifies them.

3419               	;
3420               	; 	' THE JUMP ARC IS A TABLE, not integration. That makes the 14 px apex a
3421               	; 	' property of the data rather than of a fixed-point velocity that has to
3422               	; 	' be tuned, and it keeps every comparison in the jump 8-bit and unsigned.
3423               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a depends on the apex being exactly 14.
3424               	; 	'
3425               	; 	' THIRTY FRAMES WITH NINE OF THEM AT THE APEX. The first version was 24
3426               	; 	' frames that touched 14 for only four, which made every jump a timing
3427               	; 	' test rather than a decision -- you had to leave the ground on exactly
3428               	; 	' the right frame or clip the thing you were jumping. Widening the
3429               	; 	' plateau rather than raising the apex keeps the ball arithmetic in
3430               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a intact (the apex is what that depends on) while making the
3431               	; 	' window forgiving: the player still has to CHOOSE to jump, but no longer
3432               	; 	' has to be frame-perfect about it.
3433               	; 	' THE ARC IS A TABLE, not thirty assignments -- each of those compiled to
3434               	; 	' several bytes of code, and the fixed area is the binding budget.
3435               	; 	#jat = VARPTR jarc_tbl(0)

3496               	;
3497               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR TABLE WAS 472 BYTES OF ONE REPEATED VALUE, which is a
3498               	; 	' fifth of what the fixed area had left. DEFINE COLOR copies such a table
3499               	; 	' out of ROM into all three screen thirds; writing the constant straight
3500               	; 	' into the colour table does the same job for the price of a loop, and
3501               	; 	' the loop runs once, at boot.
3502               	; 	'
3503               	; 	' The colour table is at >2000 and the VDP mirrors it once per screen
3504               	; 	' third, >800 apart. Both numbers were read out of the GENERATED assembly
3505               	; 	' -- define_color's `ai r0,>2000` and LDIRVM3's `ai r0,>0800` -- rather
3506               	; 	' than assumed, because a wrong base here would paint over the pattern
3507               	; 	' table and the failure would look like corrupt artwork.
3508               	; 	'
3509               	; 	' Paced: a few hundred VDP writes in one frame are silently dropped.
3510               	; 	' THE SCANNER'S COLOURS ARE THREE BLOCKS REPEATED SIXTEEN TIMES EACH, so
3511               	; 	' the table shipped 384 bytes to say 24 bytes' worth. Same trick as the
3512               	; 	' font: write the colour table directly. >2000 is the colour table's base
3513               	; 	' and >800 the stride between screen thirds -- the same layout DEFINE COLOR
3514               	; 	' walks for us in setup_font, which this cannot use because it is cheaper to
3515               	; 	' expand 24 bytes here than to ship 384 in the bank.
3516               	; 	' NOTHING IS UNDER THE GROUND FLOOR, SO NOTHING SHOULD BE GREEN THERE.
3517               	; 	' A floor bar is five pixels of yellow over three of the green air
3518               	; 	' belonging to the floor BELOW it (see SLAB), which is right for three of
3519               	; 	' the four bars and wrong for the last one: below floor 0 there is no
3520               	; 	' floor, only the scanner, and the green read as a strip of shop with
3521               	; 	' nothing in it.
3522               	; 	'
3523               	; 	' NO NEW CHARACTER IS NEEDED, BECAUSE THE COLOUR TABLE HAS THREE COPIES
3524               	; 	' -- one per eight screen rows -- and the bands land such that each bar
3525               	; 	' sits in a different third:
3526               	; 	'
3527               	; 	'     band 0 roof   rows  1-5    bar row  5   third 0
3528               	; 	'     band 1        rows  6-10   bar row 10   third 1
3529               	; 	'     band 2        rows 11-15   bar row 15   third 1
3530               	; 	'     band 3 GROUND rows 16-20   bar row 20   third 2
3531               	; 	'
3532               	; 	' so recolouring SLAB in third 2 alone reaches the ground floor's bar and
3533               	; 	' nothing else. The same third also holds the scanner, but the scanner
3534               	; 	' does not use these characters. This is the same mechanism that once hid
3535               	; 	' a bug for months (CLAUDE.md 3A, the blanked-in-one-third note) used
3536               	; 	' deliberately for once.
3537               	; 	'
3538               	; 	' Only the three bottom lines change, and only their BACKGROUND: SLAB has
3539               	; 	' no ink there and SLABE's brick keeps its grey.
3540               	; floor0_colour:
3541               cvb_FLOOR0_COLOUR
3542               	; 	' TWO CHARACTERS, THE SAME THREE SCAN LINES, ONE ROUTINE. Both blocks
3543               	; 	' were written out in full and differed only in which character and which
3544               	; 	' colour byte -- eleven statements twice, including the multiply-by-eight
3545               	; 	' done by doubling (`*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, which clobbers r0,
3546               	; 	' CLAUDE.md 3A).
3547               	; 	f0c = CH_SLAB
3548 AF20 0200  20 	li r0,24576   ; 96*256
     AF22 6000     
3549 AF24 D800  38 	movb r0,@cvb_F0C
     AF26 20DC     
3550               	; 	f0v = 177			' LYELL on BLACK -- no ink, so the
3551 AF28 0200  20 	li r0,45312   ; 177*256
     AF2A B100     
3552 AF2C D800  38 	movb r0,@cvb_F0V
     AF2E 20E6

3554 AF30 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     AF32 A980

3751               	;
3752               	; 	' ======================================================================
3753               	; 	' TITLE
3754               	; 	' ======================================================================
3755               	; 	' DRAWING THE TITLE AND WAITING ON IT ARE TWO ROUTINES, because the boot
3756               	; 	' does something between them: the rest of setup runs while this is on
3757               	; 	' screen. They used to be one, which is why the title could not be shown
3758               	; 	' until everything was ready.
3759               	; 	' THE TITLE IS A DISPLAY LIST IN A ROM BANK, not twelve PRINT ATs.
3760               	; 	'
3761               	; 	' CVBasic embeds a string literal in the FIXED AREA, which is the only
3762               	; 	' budget that cannot be grown -- linkticart writes exactly three loader
3763               	; 	' pages and discards the rest, and they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
3764               	; 	' >A000 rather than cart ROM. 190 characters of title text were sitting
3765               	; 	' in the scarcest place in the program.
3766               	; 	'
3767               	; 	' AND THE REAL POINT IS WHAT IT COSTS NEXT TIME. With the text in a
3768               	; 	' table, changing what the title says or where it sits is an edit to
3769               	; 	' assets/gentitle.py and a rebuild. It costs bank bytes, of which there
3770               	; 	' are thousands, instead of fixed-area bytes, of which there are tens.
3771               	; 	'
3772               	; 	' The table is `row, col, length, bytes...` with 255 to end. ROW AND
3773               	; 	' COLUMN rather than a 16-bit screen offset, because reassembling one
3774               	; 	' from two bytes needs a multiply, and on the TMS9900 MPY clobbers r0 --
3775               	; 	' the next line that reads the product's variable gets the HIGH word
3776               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). Five doublings have no such hazard and are smaller.
3777               	; title_draw:
3778               cvb_TITLE_DRAW

3902               	;
3903               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
3904               	; 	'
3905               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
3906               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
3907               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
3908               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
3909               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
3910               	; 	'
3911               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
3912               	; 	'
3913               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
3914               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,
3915               	; 	'     HardHatMack, Ms. Pac-Man, RallyX, Structris, UFO, Bust-A-Bobble --
3916               	; 	'     and not one has a calibration or has ever shown the fault.
3917               	; 	'   * It never fired on the machine this is developed on: the notice it
3918               	; 	'     prints when it detects a stuck axis has never appeared.
3919               	; 	'   * The original evidence was that the game "came up and would not
3920               	; 	'     start" -- and the first version BLOCKED until the axis cleared. That
3921               	; 	'     symptom is indistinguishable from the several input bugs since found
3922               	; 	'     and fixed for real: keys arriving at a screen that was not listening
3923               	; 	'     yet. The diagnosis was probably one of those.
3924               	; 	'
3925               	; 	' It also cost two bugs of its own: forty frames of a drawn but deaf title
3926               	; 	' screen, which swallowed the first digit of 8-3-8, and a wrong theory
3927               	; 	' about keyboard noise that led to a filter which ate real presses.
3928               	; 	'
3929               	; 	' If a stuck axis ever does appear it will be obvious -- the player will
3930               	; 	' duck or ride the lift without asking -- and the guard is in the history.
3931               	;
3932               	; title_input:
3933               cvb_TITLE_INPUT
3934               	; 	' THE PROMPT IS PRINTED HERE, NOT WITH THE REST OF THE TITLE, because
3935               	; 	' this is the moment the game starts listening -- and it is a whole
3936               	; 	' second after the title appears.
3937               	; 	'
3938               	; 	' title_draw runs early on purpose (DESIGN.md 0d-nonies) so the screen
3939               	; 	' arrives instead of filling in, but setup_rest, init_tables and the
3940               	; 	' ALPHA LOCK sample all run AFTER it. For about a second the title is up,
3941               	; 	' finished, and completely deaf. A player types 8-3-8 into that window and
3942               	; 	' the first digit lands in nothing -- then a following 3-8 completes the
3943               	; 	' code, because the 8 they typed second is still standing as state. That
3944               	; 	' is exactly how it was reported, twice, and it is not noise: it is the
3945               	; 	' screen lying about being ready.
3946               	; 	'
3947               	; 	' RallyX and Bust-A-Bobble never showed this because they draw their
3948               	; 	' titles when they are already listening. Keystone cannot -- the whole
3949               	; 	' point of the early draw is that it is early -- so the PROMPT waits

3972               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
3973               	; 	'
3974               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
3975               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
3976               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
3977               	; 	' picture.
3978               	; 	'
3979               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
3980               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
3981               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
3982               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
3983               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
3984               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
3985               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
3986               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
3987               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
3988               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
3989               	; 	' same picture.
3990               	; 	'
3991               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
3992               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
3993               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
3994               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
3995               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.

4589               	; 	'

4595               	; 	'

4597               	; 	'
4598               	; 	' His escape route ZIGZAGS -- east along floor 2 to its escalator, WEST
4599               	; 	' along floor 3 to that one, then east again along the roof to the door.
4600               	; 	' From the lift on screen 3 that is 5,120 px against the 4,208 he walked
4601               	; 	' from screen 7, so at his old 1.75 px a pass he needed 105 s of a 100 s
4602               	; 	' round: he could never escape at all, and one of the two loss conditions
4603               	; 	' would quietly have stopped existing. This block used to say exactly that
4604               	; 	' and conclude the lift was impossible. It was impossible AT THAT SPEED.
4605               	; 	'
4606               	; 	' AND QUARTER-PIXELS COULD NOT EXPRESS THE ANSWER. A quarter of a pixel
4607               	; 	' per pass is worth about TEN SECONDS of his route, so the two candidate
4608               	; 	' values straddled the buzzer with nothing in between:
4609               	; 	'
4610               	; 	'   2.00 px/pass   escapes at 102.4 s of a 100 s round   never escapes
4611               	; 	'   2.25 px/pass   escapes at  91.0 s                    nine seconds early
4612               	; 	'
4613               	; 	' Worse, 2.25 was not reachable at all: the accumulator below had two
4614               	; 	' drain steps and therefore a hard ceiling of 2 px a pass, so hsp4 = 9
4615               	; 	' silently delivered 2.00 and he fell two thirds of a screen short of his
4616               	; 	' own escape. See the accumulator comment for the full account.
4617               	; 	'
4618               	; 	' Sixteenths with three drains put the step at about 2.5 s instead of 10,
4619               	; 	' and hsp64 = 35 (2.1875 px/pass) lands him at 96.3 s of the 100 --
4620               	; 	' escaping as the timer expires, which is what was asked for.
4621               	; 	'
4622               	; 	' 35 AND NOT 34, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE PLAYER'S OWN SCREEN. Measured
4623               	; 	' in play at 34: standing on an ordinary screen he escaped with one timer
4624               	; 	' unit left, and standing on the ELEVATOR screen he ran out of clock --
4625               	; 	' same route, same constant, decided by where the player happened to be.
4626               	; 	' Everything that moves is paced per loop PASS while the clock is paced in
4627               	; 	' real FRAMES, so a busy screen slows Harry in real time and the clock does
4628               	; 	' not slow with him. A whole round measured 2,335 passes over about 98 s --
4629               	; 	' 23.8 a second, not the 25 the model assumes -- and the heavy screens are
4630               	; 	' slower again. 35 buys the margin that covers the worst of them. The
4631               	; 	' underlying split is recorded in DESIGN.md 0f-ter; this constant only
4632               	; 	' papers over it.

4857               	;
4858               	; 	' ======================================================================
4859               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
4860               	; 	' ======================================================================
4861               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
4862               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
4863               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
4864               	; 	' of running.
4865               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
4866               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
4867               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
4868               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
4869               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
4870               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
4871               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
4872               	; 	'
4873               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
4874               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
4875               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
4876               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
4877               	; 	'
4878               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
4879               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
4880               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
4881               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
4882               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
4883               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
4884               	; 	'
4885               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
4886               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
4887               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
4888               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
4889               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
4890               	; 	'
4891               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
4892               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
4893               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
4894               	; draw_screen:
4895               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN

5007               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5008               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5009               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5010               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5011               	; 	'
5012               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5013               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5014               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5015               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5016               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5017               	; 	'
5018               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5019               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5020               	; 	' above it at all.
5021               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5022               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green
5023               	; 	' under it: a beam there already ran straight into grey and needed
5024               	; 	' nothing. Giving the roof its three green rows (so the lift shaft stops
5025               	; 	' under it, like every other floor) took that away, and the top floor's
5026               	; 	' beams started falling three pixels short.
5027               	; 	'
5028               	; 	' So the roof gets its own version of the stamp. A beam HOLDS THE ROOF
5029               	; 	' UP and must reach it; the shaft merely stops beneath it.

5638               	; 			' PER KIND, not one global speed (see start_krook).
5639               	; 			' THE SPEED IS A PROPERTY OF THE KIND, and obs() only ever
5640               	; 			' held a copy of it -- set from the kind here, zeroed for a
5641               	; 			' radio below, and read in one place. upd_obst derives it
5642               	; 			' from obk() instead, which is 8 bytes of RAM back and one
5643               	; 			' fewer thing that can disagree with itself.
5644               	; 			' THEY COME FROM THE FAR SIDE. Kelly walked into this screen
5645               	; 			' from one edge, so the obstacles start at the OTHER edge and
5646               	; 			' run toward him. Crossing a seam then always presents an
5647               	; 			' ONCOMING stream, never a set of backs he has to catch up
5648               	; 			' with -- and it means the direction he is travelling is
5649               	; 			' always the direction the danger comes from.
5650               	; 			'
5651               	; 			' The table's x becomes a stagger from that edge rather than
5652               	; 			' an absolute position, and the slot index spreads them out
5653               	; 			' so they arrive in sequence instead of as one wall.
5654               	; 			'
5655               	; 			' THE SECOND ONE IS A FIXED DISTANCE BEHIND THE FIRST, AND
5656               	; 			' THAT DISTANCE IS SET BY THE JUMP.
5657               	; 			'
5658               	; 			' It used to be `(lx AND 63) + 64` -- a masked byte out of
5659               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between
5660               	; 			' the two hazards was whatever those two bytes happened to
5661               	; 			' differ by. Measured across the five populated screens it
5662               	; 			' came out 46, 46, 70, 70, 70 px. Screens 2 and 4 flank the
5663               	; 			' elevator, so the store had a visibly tighter pair on one
5664               	; 			' side of it than the other, which is exactly how it was
5665               	; 			' reported from play.
5666               	; 			'
5667               	; 			' Both numbers are too small, which is the real fault. Kelly
5668               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64
5669               	; 			' px a FRAME, and the jump is airborne 28 frames, so a jump
5670               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At
5671               	; 			' 46 or 70 there is NO screen where he can land between the
5672               	; 			' two: he clears the first and comes down on the second.
5673               	; 			'
5674               	; 			' HAZGAP is that distance with margin, and it agrees with
5675               	; 			' the original to within 4 px (see the CONST). The pairing
5676               	; 			' is now a fact about the jump rather than an accident of
5677               	; 			' two bytes. assets/checkspace.py measures it and fails the
5678               	; 			' build.
5679               	; 			' THE SECOND SLOT IS MEASURED FROM THE FIRST, not from its
5680               	; 			' own table byte. Adding HAZGAP to its own `lx AND 63` would
5681               	; 			' still leave the GAP varying by up to 63 px between screens
5682               	; 			' -- the same fault in a politer form, and the reason the two
5683               	; 			' sides of the elevator differed in the first place. Holding
5684               	; 			' slot 0's stagger and adding to that makes the gap exactly
5685               	; 			' HAZGAP on every screen, while slot 0 still lands wherever
5686               	; 			' the table puts it, so the placement variety is untouched.
5687               	; 			' DERIVED FROM THE BAND, not stored. The table used to carry
5688               	; 			' an x byte per slot; slot 1's was ignored outright (it is
5689               	; 			' `stg0 + HAZGAP`) and slot 0's only reached the game as its
5690               	; 			' low six bits. `lix` is the band index, already in hand,
5691               	; 			' and three of it spreads the thirty-two bands across the
5692               	; 			' range without lining neighbouring screens up.
